cards.front: In a histogram, what does the area of each bar represent?
cards.back: The frequency of the class.

cards.front: The formula for frequency density is $$\text{[...]}$$.
cards.back: The formula for frequency density is $$\boxed{\text{frequency density} = \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}}$$.

cards.front: What is represented on the vertical axis (y-axis) of a histogram?
cards.back: Frequency density.

cards.front: If data is measured to the nearest whole number, the class width of the interval 10–14 is [ ___ ].
cards.back: If data is measured to the nearest whole number, the class width of the interval 10–14 is 5.

cards.front: Why do the bars in a histogram typically touch?
cards.back: The data is continuous (or treated as continuous).

cards.front: How is the class width calculated for the interval 9–13 when data is rounded to the nearest integer?
cards.back: Use class boundaries 8.5 to 13.5$13.5 - 8.5 = 5$

cards.front: If two classes have the same frequency but class A is wider than class B, which bar is taller?
cards.back: Class B (the narrower class has a higher frequency density).

cards.front: How do you calculate frequency from a histogram bar?
cards.back: $$\text{class width} \times \text{frequency density}$

cards.front: When a histogram bar is measured in cm on paper, the horizontal scale links class width to [ ___ ].
cards.back: When a histogram bar is measured in cm on paper, the horizontal scale links class width to drawn width.

cards.front: When a histogram bar is measured in cm on paper, the vertical scale links frequency density to [ ___ ].
cards.back: When a histogram bar is measured in cm on paper, the vertical scale links frequency density to drawn height.

cards.front: A variable is measured to the nearest whole number. What are the class boundaries for the interval 20–22?
A class 4–8 (nearest whole number) has a frequency of 10. What is its frequency density?
cards.back: Class width = 5$10 \div 5 = 2$

cards.front: To estimate the probability of an event from a histogram, you divide the [ ___ ] by the total frequency.
cards.back: To estimate the probability of an event from a histogram, you divide the estimated frequency for the event by the total frequency.

cards.front: To estimate the probability of an event from a histogram, you divide the estimated frequency for the event by the [ ___ ].
cards.back: To estimate the probability of an event from a histogram, you divide the estimated frequency for the event by the total frequency.

cards.front: What assumption is made when a probability boundary cuts through a histogram class?
cards.back: Data is evenly spread (distributed) within that class.

cards.front: How do you estimate the frequency of a partial class where the boundary cuts through it?
cards.back: Take the fraction of the width covered by the event and multiply by the total class frequency.

cards.front: A bar has a width of 5 units and a frequency density of 2.8. What is the frequency?
The probability calculated from a histogram where boundaries cut through classes is only an [ ___ ] because the exact distribution of values within classes is unknown.
cards.back: The probability calculated from a histogram where boundaries cut through classes is only an estimate because the exact distribution of values within classes is unknown.

cards.front: In a histogram, the bar for 9–13 has a class width of 5 and a drawn width of 2.5 cm. What is the horizontal scale?
cards.back: 0.5 cm per unit ($2.5 \div 5$)

cards.front: If frequency density 2.4 is represented by a drawn height of 3.6 cm, what is the vertical scale?
cards.back: 1.5 cm per unit ($3.6 \div 2.4$)

cards.front: What is the primary reason for using a histogram instead of a standard bar chart?
cards.back: The data is grouped and the class widths are unequal.
